purpose: Twelve new country features for smallest states and underrepresented African and Asian countries. Site status distinguished explicitly as UNESCO World Heritage inscription, UNESCO tentative, UNESCO biosphere reserve, or national protected area.
rights: Original educational text and source citations only. No photo permissions or binaries.
preservation: No changes to IDs, shop, localStorage, profile access, XP or purchases.

records.hook: San Marino — Historic Centre and Mount Titano

sections.title: A capital on Mount Titano
sections.body: San Marino's historic centre sits high on Mount Titano, above the surrounding hills of the Italian peninsula. Towers, defensive walls and a compact street network reveal why this exposed position mattered historically. The World Heritage site includes an inhabited political centre, rather than a deserted fortress. Its visual character depends both on the masonry of the town and the mountainous setting below.

sections.title: An enduring republic
sections.body: San Marino's institutions trace their history across many centuries, and the city has continued to serve as the republic's capital. Palaces, public squares and the surrounding fortifications record changes in civic life. Its history should not be represented as politically unchanged in every detail since medieval times. Institutions and buildings have been adapted, reconstructed and interpreted by successive generations.

sections.title: Defence and architecture
sections.body: The three towers associated with Mount Titano are prominent features of the skyline. Their positions are part of a wider defensive landscape in which steep slopes offered a natural advantage. Religious and civic buildings added other functions to the hilltop town. Some restored features reflect nineteenth- and twentieth-century ideas about how a historic republic should present its past.

sections.title: A living historic place
sections.body: The challenge of conservation is to protect the landscape and built fabric while allowing residents and institutions to function. Tourism brings attention and income, but can change commercial activity and street use. San Marino demonstrates how a small state's national identity may be closely linked with the continuing role of one historic urban centre.

sections.title: An independent state within Rome
sections.body: Vatican City occupies a small area inside the city of Rome. Its World Heritage property coincides with the territory of the state and includes religious buildings, museums, gardens and working institutions. This unusual arrangement means that an internationally important cultural landscape also has a continuing governmental and religious function. The surrounding streets of Rome connect the site to a much larger urban history.

sections.title: Architecture over centuries
sections.body: St Peter's Basilica and its great colonnaded square are among the best-known elements, yet their construction involved many architects and separate building campaigns. Earlier archaeological remains lie beneath later structures, while Renaissance and Baroque additions changed the complex. The visual unity seen by visitors is the result of successive projects rather than a design completed all at once.

sections.title: Art, libraries and knowledge
sections.body: Frescoes, sculpture and manuscript collections preserve evidence of different periods of artistic patronage and scholarship. The Vatican Museums and Library have distinct histories, and access to their collections has changed over time. Although the site's religious importance is central, its significance to the study of art and architecture extends beyond one community of believers.

sections.title: Continuing use and conservation
sections.body: Religious ceremonies, visitors and the daily work of institutions take place amid fragile art and historic buildings. Managing crowds and conserving materials are ongoing responsibilities. Vatican City illustrates how heritage can remain both symbolically important and actively used. A visitor should recognise the people and institutions maintaining the site, not see it merely as a museum of famous masterpieces.

records.hook: Bhutan — Dzongs: religious and civic fortresses

sections.title: Fortresses in Himalayan valleys
sections.body: Bhutan's dzongs are large fortified complexes built in strategic locations, often above rivers or on hillsides. Their thick outer walls and substantial courtyards combine practical defence with distinctive religious architecture. Several historic dzongs are part of Bhutan's UNESCO Tentative List, which proposes sites for possible future nomination. Tentative status is not the same as having World Heritage inscription.

sections.title: Religious and political functions
sections.body: The buildings served both Buddhist monastic communities and systems of local administration. Temples, meeting spaces and residences occupied different parts of the same complex, creating a shared centre of spiritual and civic authority. Their significance cannot be understood through battlements alone. Architecture and public institutions developed together as Bhutan's political organisation changed.

sections.title: Craft and construction
sections.body: Timber carving, painted details and stone masonry demonstrate specialist building traditions. Builders had to respond to steep terrain, weather and the available materials. Fire and other damage have prompted repairs or rebuilding at some sites, so the structures visible now contain multiple layers of work. The most useful approach is to consider preservation as a continuing tradition rather than assume no changes have occurred.

sections.title: Living institutions today
sections.body: Some dzongs still accommodate religious activity and government functions. Visitors therefore encounter places used by communities, not vacant palaces. Conservation must balance access, the protection of artwork and the requirements of ongoing ceremonies. These Himalayan structures show how the placement of buildings, cultural values and practical administration can become closely linked over several centuries.

sections.title: A salt lake below sea level
sections.body: Lake Assal lies within an arid volcanic landscape in Djibouti, in the geological region of the Afar Depression. It occupies a basin well below sea level, where water and minerals interact in unusual conditions. White salt deposits contrast with dark rock and surrounding desert. The lake is listed on Djibouti's UNESCO Tentative List, rather than being a currently inscribed World Heritage site.

sections.title: Water, evaporation and salt
sections.body: Strong evaporation and limited outflow help explain the accumulation of very saline water and salt deposits. Geological processes shape the basin and the surrounding terrain. These features are useful for studying mineral formation and the interaction between climate and topography. A salt lake is not an ordinary freshwater reservoir, and its ecological conditions differ sharply from those of more familiar lakes.

sections.title: People and mineral resources
sections.body: Communities have used salt from the region, and transport routes connect the basin with the wider country. Resource use can provide livelihoods while also raising questions about environmental management. The landscape should not be portrayed as empty just because vegetation is sparse. Cultural connections, work and movement form part of its history.

sections.title: A fragile and striking environment
sections.body: Visitors may be attracted by the appearance of salt and water, but physical geography is the main lesson of the site. Conservation discussions must account for extraction, access and the water balance. Lake Assal demonstrates how tectonics, evaporation and human activity combine to shape a landscape that looks unlike most lakes elsewhere in the world.

sections.title: An exceptionally old mining landscape
sections.body: Ngwenya lies in the highlands of Eswatini, where iron-rich deposits were worked long before modern industry. Archaeological evidence associated with ochre extraction extends back into the Middle Stone Age. The site appears on the country's UNESCO Tentative List, a status indicating possible future nomination, not current inscription. Its importance lies in the deep history of human use of geological resources.

sections.title: Pigments as valuable materials
sections.body: Red haematite and other minerals could be collected and prepared for different purposes, including pigments. Archaeologists examine traces of past extraction to understand technology and decision-making among earlier communities. An ancient mine is not automatically comparable with a modern industrial excavation. Scale, tools and social organisation differed significantly, while some interpretations remain matters of research.

sections.title: Different episodes of extraction
sections.body: The landscape also contains evidence of much later mining activity. Separating these periods is essential because modern disturbances can affect older archaeological remains. Geological formations, waste deposits and access routes provide different clues to how people worked the area. Conservation has to consider what excavation reveals and what future generations might still need to study.

sections.title: A long view of human technology
sections.body: Ngwenya is a reminder that resource use and technical knowledge began many thousands of years before factories or mechanical mining. The surrounding hills, local communities and changing land uses all matter to interpretation. Its proposed heritage value comes from connecting geological materials to the history of people who selected and processed them over time.

records.hook: São Tomé and Príncipe — Príncipe Island Biosphere Reserve

sections.title: A volcanic island in the Gulf of Guinea
sections.body: Príncipe is an oceanic island with steep volcanic terrain, tropical forest and small settlements. UNESCO recognises its terrestrial and surrounding marine environments as a biosphere reserve. This is a designation within the Man and the Biosphere Programme, not an inscription on the World Heritage List. The combination of land and sea habitats helps explain the island's ecological importance.

sections.title: Isolation and distinctive wildlife
sections.body: Oceanic islands can develop species and communities that differ from nearby continental environments. Forest, coastal habitats and the surrounding ocean form overlapping ecological systems. Changes in land cover or marine water quality can therefore influence wildlife well beyond a particular field or beach. Researchers examine biodiversity along with the geography that shaped the island over geological time.

sections.title: Communities and land use
sections.body: People live and work within the biosphere landscape, where agriculture, fishing and services can all affect conservation priorities. Historical plantation activities changed parts of the environment and economy. The reserve concept aims to connect ecological protection with sustainable human activity rather than exclude all local uses. Decisions about land and resources require community participation.

sections.title: Connecting mountains and sea
sections.body: A view down from a forested ridge shows why a conservation boundary drawn only around land would be incomplete. Rainwater flows into streams and eventually coastal water, carrying effects from activities uphill. Príncipe provides a compact example of how biodiversity, volcanic geology and everyday livelihoods are interdependent in island environments.

sections.title: Island and sea in one protected area
sections.body: Mwali, also called Mohéli, is one of the Comoros islands in the Mozambique Channel. Its UNESCO biosphere reserve encompasses land and surrounding marine areas, reflecting the close relationship between coastal villages, reefs and inland environments. Biosphere-reserve recognition differs from World Heritage inscription. The island provides a manageable setting in which to study interactions between people and multiple ecosystems.

sections.title: Reefs, mangroves and seagrass
sections.body: The coast includes lagoons, marine vegetation and coral habitats that support fish and other wildlife. Mangroves and seagrasses contribute to coastal ecology by providing shelter and places for young animals to develop. Inland streams and land use can affect coastal water quality. Protecting one spectacular coral site without the surrounding habitats would give an incomplete approach to conservation.

sections.title: Natural and human history
sections.body: Volcanic origins helped shape the island, while communities have long depended on marine resources and local cultivation. Fishing and tourism may provide income but also require agreed rules. Different residents can experience conservation restrictions differently, so management needs clear communication and involvement from those affected. The reserve also belongs to a wider regional marine ecosystem.

sections.title: A connected conservation model
sections.body: Water, wildlife and human activities cross boundaries between forest, village and sea. Monitoring should therefore include more than the number of visitors or the condition of individual beaches. Mwali is useful for understanding the broader purpose of biosphere reserves: encouraging approaches that consider ecosystems and sustainable livelihoods together.

sections.title: Rainforest in the Upper Guinean region
sections.body: The Gola-Tiwai Complex combines protected forest landscapes in south-eastern Sierra Leone, including Gola and Tiwai Island. The UNESCO World Heritage site was inscribed in 2025 for its ecological importance. Dense forest, rivers and varied habitats form part of a larger West African biodiversity region. The protected components should not be mistaken for one continuous fenced reserve.

sections.title: Species and ecological processes
sections.body: The forests provide habitat for primates, birds and many smaller organisms. Some species are threatened, while others have limited geographical distributions. Conserving such biodiversity depends on maintaining habitat quality, connectivity and natural processes. Research involves monitoring vegetation, animal populations and environmental pressures, rather than assuming that a forest viewed from above is unchanged.

sections.title: Communities across the landscape
sections.body: People living around protected areas use land and resources in different ways. Conservation management has involved local communities, authorities and conservation organisations. Decisions about access, livelihoods and agricultural pressure can affect the long-term effectiveness of protection. The natural heritage of the forest cannot be separated from the people who live near and help manage it.

sections.title: Why a new inscription matters
sections.body: Gola-Tiwai illustrates the international significance of West Africa's remaining Upper Guinean forests. Its recognition in 2025 provides an opportunity to discuss both ecological value and the practical responsibilities of caring for the site. Preserving a complex ecosystem involves continued scientific work and community cooperation, not simply adding a name to a heritage list.

sections.title: A rainforest across a political border
sections.body: Liberia's Gola Rainforest National Park protects part of the Upper Guinean forest region close to Sierra Leone. The neighbouring country has related protected forests, making this a landscape where ecology extends across national boundaries. Liberia's Gola park is on UNESCO's Tentative List, not currently a separately inscribed World Heritage property. That distinction is important when describing its international recognition.

sections.title: A rich forest community
sections.body: Moist forest habitats support birds, primates, plants and many other organisms, including species of conservation concern. Rivers and changes in terrain create different ecological conditions within the forest. Researchers examine habitat distribution and animal populations while recognising gaps in the available evidence. A forest can appear continuous while roads or other disturbances reduce connections that some species need.

sections.title: Protection and livelihoods
sections.body: Communities surrounding the park depend on land and forest resources in different ways. Management requires discussion of farming, livelihoods and rules governing access. Cooperation with neighbouring protected areas offers possibilities for supporting wildlife that moves across the border. The human geography of the region matters alongside the protection of trees and animals.

sections.title: Forests in a changing climate
sections.body: Tropical forests store carbon and influence local water processes, although their conservation value is much wider than carbon alone. Land-use pressure, illegal extraction and climate changes can create overlapping risks. Gola is a useful case study of cross-border conservation and why protecting ecosystems often requires agreements among local communities, scientists and governments.

sections.title: Rainforest in eastern Brunei
sections.body: Ulu Temburong National Park occupies part of Brunei's Temburong district on the island of Borneo. The landscape is dominated by tropical rainforest, hills and rivers rather than the urban coastal environments sometimes associated with the country. Brunei's official tourism information describes the park's varied lowland and upland forest. The park is not a UNESCO World Heritage inscription.

sections.title: A forest with many levels
sections.body: Rainforest habitats vary between riverbanks, slopes and the canopy above. Trees compete for light, while insects, birds and mammals use different parts of the environment. Observing the canopy can reveal relationships that are difficult to see from a forest floor. Such habitats depend on rainfall, soil and the continuity of vegetation, and can be affected by land use outside formal boundaries.

sections.title: People and forest knowledge
sections.body: Communities in the wider Temburong region have cultural and economic connections with rivers and forest landscapes. Guided visitors encounter these environments through established routes and managed facilities. Access systems help limit some disturbance, but tourism can also create impacts if it is not carefully planned. Local knowledge and livelihoods belong in any conservation discussion.

sections.title: A wider Borneo perspective
sections.body: The park forms part of a much larger island with differing land uses and jurisdictions. Understanding its significance means comparing protected forest with neighbouring landscapes, not treating the reserve as a self-contained ecosystem. Ulu Temburong offers a useful opportunity to examine rainforest structure, catchments, biodiversity and the decisions involved in protecting tropical habitats.

sections.title: A network of low coral islands
sections.body: The Maldives consists of atolls and islands surrounded by the Indian Ocean. Baa Atoll lies in the country's central-western region and is recognised by UNESCO as a biosphere reserve. This designation is separate from World Heritage inscription. Reef channels, lagoons and tiny islands create different environments within a relatively small geographical area.

sections.title: The living framework of a reef
sections.body: Coral animals build structures that provide habitat for fish and invertebrates. Seagrass beds and mangroves add different nursery and coastal habitats, while water movement connects organisms across reefs. Atolls depend on complex relationships between biological growth, waves and sediment. Their visible shape is the outcome of long processes rather than a permanent barrier unaffected by ocean conditions.

sections.title: Manta rays and ocean productivity
sections.body: The reserve is known for gatherings of manta rays associated with plankton-rich waters. Understanding where and when animals feed requires attention to tides, currents and nutrient conditions. Scientific research helps connect these behaviours with protection measures. Wildlife tourism can support awareness, but activities around feeding animals need careful management to minimise disturbance.

sections.title: People and a low-lying environment
sections.body: Fishing, tourism and settlement are part of the atoll's modern life. Changes in sea conditions and coastal development affect both residents and habitats. Conservation therefore involves practical decisions about water, waste and marine resource use. Baa Atoll illustrates the connection between coral-reef ecology and the everyday challenges faced by communities living on small oceanic islands.

records.hook: Timor-Leste — Nino Konis Santana Biosphere Reserve

sections.title: Land and sea at Timor's eastern end
sections.body: Nino Konis Santana occupies part of eastern Timor-Leste, where coastal habitats meet forested and upland environments. UNESCO designated the area the country's first biosphere reserve in 2026. That recognition does not mean it is an inscribed World Heritage site. The reserve includes a mosaic of coral reefs, wetlands, seagrass and terrestrial ecosystems connected by short distances.

sections.title: Biodiversity in the Coral Triangle
sections.body: The waters around the region belong to the wider Coral Triangle, an area known for extensive marine biodiversity. Reef fish, coral species and other organisms depend on different habitats through their lives. Rivers and land use can affect coastal water quality, creating connections between forest management and marine protection. Conservation cannot be considered only below the waterline.

sections.title: Cultural landscapes and knowledge
sections.body: Communities have long histories in the region, including traditions associated with land and the sea. UNESCO's biosphere designation recognises the relevance of local knowledge and livelihoods. Scientific research and community participation can provide complementary perspectives on ecological change. A description limited to beaches and wildlife would miss these social relationships.

sections.title: A recent conservation milestone
sections.body: The 2026 designation provides a framework for supporting ecological protection alongside sustainable development. Implementation still requires resources, monitoring and ongoing local decisions. Nino Konis Santana offers an example of how a newly recognised biosphere reserve can connect biological research, cultural heritage and practical management in a country with extensive coastal environments.
